definition: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is a hypothesized process in which artificial general intelligence (AGI) systems rewrite their own computer code, causing an intelligence explosion resulting from enhancing their own capabilities and intellectual capacity, theoretically resulting in superintelligence.
details: Numerous attempts at RSI have been made, none so far showing any sign of intelligence explosion or superintelligence. The development of recursive self-improvement raises significant ethical and safety concerns, as such systems may evolve in unforeseen ways and could potentially surpass human control or understanding.

explainer.lead: A hypothesized process in which AGI systems rewrite their own code, enhancing their capabilities and intellectual capacity and theoretically resulting in superintelligence. It matters for both capability forecasts and safety.

tiers.eli5: Picture a mechanic who can upgrade their own tools, then use the better tools to upgrade them again — in theory getting better faster and faster.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers invoke it when reasoning about risk and control; the pitfall is overstating it, since numerous attempts have shown no sign of an intelligence explosion or superintelligence.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined as AGI systems rewriting their own computer code to enhance their own capabilities and intellectual capacity, theoretically resulting in superintelligence. No attempt so far has shown any sign of intelligence explosion or superintelligence.

explainer.example: A hypothetical AGI that edits its own code to boost its reasoning, then uses the improved reasoning to edit further.
